analysis.one_liner: Makes Medicare coverage of telehealth visits permanent, letting seniors get care by phone or video from anywhere.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to make Medicare telehealth rules permanent drew 244 cosponsors — 182 of 217 House Democrats and 62 of 223 House Republicans — but has had no hearing, markup, or vote since being referred to two committees in June 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare only pays for telehealth under special rules: patients generally had to be in a clinic, not at home, and the looser COVID-era rules have been extended only in short-term patches. This bill removes the location limits permanently, lets more kinds of clinicians bill for telehealth, ends the requirement that mental-health patients first have an in-person visit, lets community health centers, rural clinics, and Native American health facilities bill as telehealth sites, and lets the government loosen rules during declared health emergencies. It pairs the expansion with anti-fraud tools, including $3 million a year for HHS inspectors and new tracking of unusual telehealth billing.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — especially seniors in rural areas, people with limited mobility or transportation, and mental-health patients — who could see a doctor by phone or video from home permanently rather than through short-term extensions. Community health centers, rural clinics, and Native American health facilities gain a new way to reach and bill for patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare seniors, rural patients, and telehealth providers

how_it_helps.text: Removes the rule that a Medicare patient must normally be at a qualifying clinic to use telehealth, effective October 1, 2025, so beneficiaries can get covered telehealth from home anywhere in the country.
Repeals the requirement that telemental health services be preceded by an in-person visit within six months, removing a major barrier for mental-health patients.

Lets federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics be paid under their regular payment systems for telehealth they provide, and exempts Indian Health Service, tribal, and Native Hawaiian health facilities from the originating-site rules.

Expands the types of practitioners who can furnish telehealth, letting the Secretary waive practitioner limits when clinically appropriate, and allows telehealth to be used for hospice recertification.

Pairs the expansion with program-integrity measures: $3 million per year for the HHS Inspector General to audit telehealth (fiscal years 2026-2030), new identification of significant outlier telehealth billers, and clarified anti-kickback rules for technology given to beneficiaries.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through Medicare: permanent telehealth coverage increases federal spending, and the bill includes no dedicated offset or pay-for in its text; the bill also authorizes additional appropriations for oversight and beneficiary and provider training.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes telehealth coverage permanent and authorizes new appropriations without any offsetting savings, so it increases federal Medicare spending; earlier temporary telehealth extensions were the subject of repeated budget fights over exactly this cost.

Expanded telehealth carries real fraud risk — the bill's own Title II exists because of it, directing Medicare to flag significant outlier billing patterns such as inflated visit lengths and duplicate billing, and funding HHS Inspector General audits of telehealth services.

The bill lets Medicare pay Federally qualified health centers and rural clinics under their regular payment systems for telehealth, and provides that telehealth-related technology costs count as allowable costs in those payment calculations, which adds new payment obligations on top of existing fee-for-service telehealth payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For rural, homebound, and mental-health patients the access gains are real and the bill's anti-fraud title is more than window dressing — it funds actual audits and targets outlier billers. The honest cost is money: permanence plus new payment channels and oversight all add federal spending with no pay-for, which is precisely why telehealth permanence has repeatedly stalled in past Congresses. The design is reasonable; the financing question is unresolved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees in June 2025, and neither committee has acted on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson (D-CA) introduced the bill on June 26, 2025, joined by original cosponsors Rep. David Schweikert (R-AZ), Rep. Doris Matsui (D-CA), and Rep. Troy Balderson (R-OH).

It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Committee on Ways and Means, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — since that referral.
It attracted 244 cosponsors, including 182 of 217 House Democrats and 62 of 223 House Republicans, making it one of the most broadly supported health bills in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet: the bill simply sits in committee while Medicare telehealth rules continue on their existing temporary footing, and the telehealth and provider industries await certainty that only congressional action can give.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CONNECT for Health Act of 2025 on June 26, 2025.

for.name: Reps. Schweikert, Matsui, and Balderson
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in June 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing or markup — as of the latest recorded action history.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in June 2025 and has taken no further action on the bill in the recorded history.

sides.party_line_note: Support is genuinely two-sided: 182 of 217 House Democrats and 62 of 223 House Republicans signed on, and the original cosponsors included two Republicans; no member has opposed it on the record, and no vote has occurred.

industries.note: The bill makes telehealth a permanent, rather than temporary, channel for delivering Medicare care, locking in a durable Medicare billing stream for telehealth providers and platforms. Patients gain access at the same time, and the bill imposes fraud oversight on the same industry it entrenches.

industries.industry: Federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics
industries.note: They become permanently payable as distant-site telehealth providers under their existing prospective payment systems, expanding revenue while serving patients who otherwise travel far for care.

The bill clarifies fraud-and-abuse law so providers can furnish telehealth and remote-monitoring technologies directly to beneficiaries without triggering anti-kickback penalties, opening a new channel for equipment supplied to seniors — subject to Secretary-defined conditions and a bar on use in advertising or solicitation.

industries.industry: Medicare fraud investigators (HHS Office of Inspector General)
industries.note: The bill authorizes $3 million per year for fiscal 2026-2030 for audits and enforcement of telehealth billing, and requires Medicare to flag significant outlier billers — oversight aimed at a fraud problem the expansion could otherwise worsen.

analysis.trajectory: Telehealth is one of the few health issues with this level of bipartisan House support, and its most realistic path is being folded into a year-end Medicare or health-extender package, possibly as a shorter extension rather than full permanence; as a standalone bill, it has seen no committee action in the six months since referral, and cost concerns without a pay-for are the usual reason such permanence bills stall.
